## Grammar before pronunciation

Last class: **PAST** and **-ed** can come apart.

Grammatical encoding: selecting words and constructing syntax.

| Processing | What gets specified |
|---|---|
| Functional | Lemmas and grammatical functions |
| Positional | Word order and inflectional slots |

Phonological encoding supplies the sound forms.

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, I, Fig. 1
:::

::: {.notes}
Last week we looked at *they needed to be maded*. The speaker had already
retrieved *made*, which is past, and still attached another *-ed*. That told us
that the feature PAST and the suffix *-ed* are two separate things in
production.

Bock and Levelt give us a larger picture of where those two things live. They
call the grammatical part of production grammatical encoding, and they split it
in two. Functional processing selects lemmas and assigns grammatical functions
like subject and object. Positional processing puts things in order and sets up
slots for inflections. The sounds come after both.

One warning: these labels do not match Levelt's levels from last week one to
one, so check what each author puts under each name.

In the second half of class, you will be the participants in an experiment
about one claim in this reading: where the *to* in *listen to* comes from. Then
you will design your own version.
:::

## Event roles in the message

*She was handing him some broccoli.*

| Event role | Participant |
|---|---|
| Agent | The person doing the handing |
| Recipient | The person receiving the broccoli |
| Theme | The broccoli being transferred |

The message also specifies a **past, ongoing event**.

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, I
:::

::: {.notes}
Take their example sentence, *She was handing him some broccoli*. Before any
grammar, the speaker has an event in mind. Someone does the handing: that is the
agent. Someone receives something: the recipient. The broccoli is the thing
being transferred: the theme. These are roles in the event. They say nothing
yet about subject or object.

The message also includes that the event is in the past and ongoing. English
expresses that with *was* plus *-ing*, but at the message level there is only
the meaning.
:::

## Function assignment

*She was handing him some broccoli.*

| Selected lemma | Assigned function in this example |
|---|---|
| Feminine pronoun | Subject / nominative |
| Masculine pronoun | Dative |
| *broccoli* | Accusative |
| *hand* | Main verb |

Lexical selection and function assignment make up **functional processing**.

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, I
:::

::: {.notes}
Here is the same sentence with grammatical functions. The feminine pronoun is
assigned the subject function, which is nominative. The masculine pronoun gets
what they call the dative function, *broccoli* gets the accusative, and *hand*
is the main verb. Selecting the lemmas and assigning these functions together
make up functional processing.

They give a possible error: *He was handing her some broccoli*. Why do we get
*he* and *her* in this error? Why not *Him was handing she*?

*[Pause for answers.]*

The functions were swapped. The masculine pronoun ended up with the subject
function, so it comes out as *he*. The feminine pronoun ended up with the dative
function, so it comes out as *her*. The form of each pronoun depends on the
function it received.

They also say that the numbered steps in their description are there to explain
the model. We should not read them as a fixed order of operations.
:::

## Positional processing

*She was handing him some broccoli.*

| Component | What gets specified |
|---|---|
| Constituent assembly | Phrase structure and word order |
| Inflection | Morphological slots within that structure |

In *handing*: **stem + affix**, expressing the progressive feature.

Phonological encoding supplies the sounds.

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, I
:::

::: {.notes}
Assigning functions does not yet give you the order of the words. That is
positional processing. Constituent assembly builds the phrase structure and
fixes word order. Inflection fills the smaller slots inside that structure, like
the stem *hand* plus the affix *-ing* in *handing*. The sounds still come later.

Their evidence that inflections are positioned separately from stems is a kind
of error called stranding. A speaker meant to say *You ended up ordering some
fish dish* and said *You ordered up ending some fish dish*. The stems *end* and
*order* swapped places, and *-ed* and *-ing* stayed where they were.
:::

## Two assumptions

- **Restricted information flow:** each level is influenced by the level
  immediately above it.
- **Incrementality:** processing can begin on part of an utterance before the
  preceding level has finished the rest.

::: {.prompt}
Does selection before pronunciation require planning the whole sentence first?
:::

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, I
:::

::: {.notes}
Bock and Levelt make two assumptions. The first is restricted information flow:
each level only gets information from the level directly above it. That means
the sound of a word cannot influence which lemma gets selected. They call this a
very strong position, and we will come back to it with mixed errors.

The second is incrementality. A level can start working on the first part of a
sentence while the level above it is still working on the rest.

So here is a question. If we select lemmas before we pronounce them, do we have
to plan the whole sentence before we start talking?

*[Pause for answers.]*

No. For a single word, the lemma comes before the sound. How much of the
sentence we plan at once is a separate question, and incrementality says we can
start before the rest is ready. This is the planning scope question from Griffin
and Ferreira.
:::

## Selecting a lemma

| Representation | Information |
|---|---|
| Concept | SHEEP: an animal, has wool |
| Lemma | *sheep*: noun |
| Lexeme | Morphological and phonological form |

- Activating SHEEP also activates related concepts, including GOAT.
- Their lemmas become active. Selection depends on relative activation.

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, II.A; Roelofs 1992
:::

::: {.notes}
Bock and Levelt separate three kinds of information about a word. The concept
SHEEP includes things like being an animal and having wool. The lemma *sheep*
has the grammatical information: that it is a noun, and for other words things
like gender or which arguments a verb takes. The lexeme has the form, its
morphology and its sounds.

So a lemma is more than a stem without its suffix. The fact that *listen* takes
*to* is stored in the lemma for *listen*. We will use that in today's
experiment.

When you think of SHEEP, related concepts like GOAT get activated too, and so do
their lemmas. Which lemma gets selected depends on how active *sheep* is compared
to the other active lemmas.
:::

## Relative activation

For a given selection interval:

$$
P(\text{select sheep}) =
\frac{\text{activation of sheep}}
{\text{total activation of lemmas in the experimental set}}
$$

::: {.fragment}
More activation of *goat*, with *sheep* unchanged: a lower probability of
selecting *sheep* in that interval.
:::

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, II.A; Roelofs 1992
:::

::: {.notes}
This is Roelofs's version of how a lemma gets selected. In any short time
interval, the chance of selecting *sheep* is its activation divided by the total
activation of all the lemmas in the set.

Let me put some made-up numbers on the board, only for the arithmetic. Say
*sheep* has 6 and *goat* has 2. The chance of selecting *sheep* is 6 out of 8.
Now leave *sheep* at 6 and raise *goat* to 6. The chance is 6 out of 12.

*[Advance.]*

The activation of *sheep* did not change, and its chance of being selected in
each interval went down. A lower chance per interval means it takes longer on
average to select it. That is one explanation for semantic interference from
Griffin and Ferreira: a related word like *goat* slows down naming a picture of
a sheep.
:::

## Retrieving gender or saying the word?

Frequent picture names are produced faster. Dutch task: judge the name's gender, or name the picture.

| After repeated presentations | Word frequency effect |
|---|---|
| Gender judgment | Disappears |
| Picture naming | Persists |

The authors locate the persistent effect primarily at the **lexeme** level.

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, II.C; Jescheniak & Levelt, cited as in press
:::

::: {.notes}
People name pictures with frequent names faster than pictures with rare names.
The question is where that frequency effect comes from: the lemma or the
lexeme.

Jescheniak and Levelt tested this with Dutch speakers. Dutch nouns have one of
two grammatical genders. Speakers saw pictures and did one of two tasks. In one
task, they named the picture. In the other, they pressed one of two buttons to
indicate the gender of the picture's name, without saying the name.

Each picture came up three times in each task. At first, both tasks showed a
frequency effect. In the gender task, the effect was gone by the third time. In
naming, it stayed. Gender is information in the lemma, and naming needs the
form, so they conclude that the lasting frequency effect is at the lexeme.

There is a general point here for designing experiments: a button press can get
at grammatical information about a word without asking anyone to say the word.
:::

## Can sounds affect selection?

Mixed error: *oyster* for *lobster*, similar in meaning **and** sound.

| Account | Why mixed errors are frequent |
|---|---|
| Feedback | Sound activation influences selection |
| Monitoring | Similar errors are less likely to be detected |

::: {.prompt}
What evidence would distinguish producing more errors from detecting fewer?
:::

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, II.B and II.C; Dell & Reich 1981; Levelt 1989
:::

::: {.notes}
A mixed error is an error where the wrong word is related to the intended word
in both meaning and sound, like *oyster* for *lobster*. Dell and Reich found
that these errors are more common than you would expect if meaning errors and
sound errors had separate sources.

There are two explanations. The first is feedback: the sounds of *oyster* send
activation back up and help it get selected. That would break the restricted
information flow assumption. The second is monitoring: speakers check their
own speech before and while they say it, and an error that is similar to the
intended word in both meaning and sound is more likely to get past that check.
Bock and Levelt argue that feedback may be unnecessary, and monitoring is one of
their reasons.

What kind of evidence would tell apart producing more of these errors from
catching fewer of them?

*[Pause for answers.]*

Counting errors in a corpus cannot separate the two, because a corpus only
contains the errors that got out. You would need a way to see errors that were
produced and then caught, or a task that changes how much speakers can monitor
themselves.
:::

## How is *to* selected?

*Listen **to** the radio.*

- *Listen* has grammatical requirements.
- Those requirements lead to selection of *to*.
- The authors call this **indirect election**.

::: {.prompt}
What would an account based only on lexical concepts leave unexplained here?
:::

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, II.A
:::

::: {.notes}
In *listen to the radio*, the word *to* does not express a concept of its own.
Bock and Levelt say that the lemma for *listen* requires *to*, so *to* gets
activated through *listen*. They call this indirect election.

What would a model miss if it only connected concepts to words?

*[Pause for answers.]*

It would have no route to *to*, because there is no concept for *to* to come
from.

This is the Property 9 question from Griffin and Ferreira: is a function word
chosen through the grammar of another word, or does it come with a frame? If
indirect election is right, *to* should go wherever *listen* goes. Today's
experiment tests that.
:::

## What stayed when the nouns exchanged?

Intended: *a **floor** full of **holes***

Produced: *a **hole** full of **floors***

::: {.fragment}
The nouns exchanged. Plural marking stayed in the second position.
:::

::: {.fragment .prompt}
What would a whole noun phrase exchange have produced?
:::

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, II.B, example 11; Fromkin 1973
:::

::: {.notes}
Here is a speech error from Fromkin. The speaker meant to say *a floor full of
holes* and said *a hole full of floors*.

*[Advance.]*

The nouns *floor* and *hole* traded places. The plural *-s* stayed in the second
position, and the article *a* stayed at the beginning.

If the whole noun phrases had traded places, what would the speaker have said?

*[Pause for answers, then advance.]*

*Holes full of a floor*. The article and the plural would have gone with their
nouns. Bock and Levelt say this is typical of clear word exchanges: the rest of
the phrase stays behind, including small grammatical elements. Later in the
chapter they cite Stemberger (1985), who found inflectional affixes stranded in
88.9% of the errors where stranding was possible.

This is the same kind of evidence as *maded* last week. The plural and the noun
it attaches to are placed separately.
:::

## Possible endings for trial 2 {.trial-slide}

:::: {.trial-sequence}
::: {.trial-card .previous}
[Trial 1: you said]{.trial-label}

I remember the musician that Maya **heard**.
:::

::: {.trial-arrow aria-hidden="true"}
→
:::

::: {.trial-card .current}
[Trial 2: target]{.trial-label}

I met the singer that Katie **listened to**.
:::
::::

| Trial 2 ending | What changed |
|---|---|
| *listened to* | Nothing |
| *heard* | Verb carried over |
| *listened* | Verb kept, *to* lost |
| *heard to* | Verb carried over, *to* kept |

::: {.prompt}
Which ending would show that *to* comes from *listen*? Which would show a reused structure?
:::

::: {.notes}
On the first trial you said *I remember the musician that Maya heard*. On the
second trial, the target was *I met the singer that Katie listened to*. If the
first trial affected the second, the second sentence could have ended in a few
ways. *Listened to* is the target. *Heard* means the verb from the first trial
came back. *Listened* without *to* means you kept the verb and lost *to*. *Heard
to* means the verb from the first trial came back and *to* stayed.

Which ending would show that *to* comes from *listen*? Which would show that you
reused the structure of the first sentence?

*[Pause for answers.]*

If *to* comes from the lemma for *listen*, then *to* goes wherever *listen* goes.
An effect of the first trial would show up as *heard*, the whole verb, and
*listened* by itself should be rare.

The other possibility is that you reused the structure of the first sentence, a
verb followed directly by its object. Speakers tend to repeat structures they
have just used, even with different words (Bock and Loebell 1990). In that case
you could keep *listened* and still drop *to*.

*Heard to* would be interesting: the verb from the first trial inside the
structure of the second.

One more possibility for *listened* without *to*: you might have planned *to* and
then not pronounced it. The ending by itself does not tell us which of these
happened.
:::

object, *to* should be missing more often after trials 1 and 7 than after trials
4 and 10. If *to* only comes from the lemma of the target verb, those rows should
not differ in missing *to*. An effect of the trial before would show up as a
different verb instead, most likely in row 2, where *heard* is close in meaning
to *listened*.

Rows 2 and 5 have verbs close in meaning to the target, and rows 8 and 11 do not.
Comparing them tells us whether similarity in meaning matters.

Here are the problems with what we just did. There is one sentence per row, and
each row has a different target verb, so a difference between rows could come
from the verbs themselves. Everyone spoke at once, so I heard some errors and
missed others. Raising a hand counts only the errors you noticed yourself.

What would you change to make this a real experiment?

*[Take answers: several sentences per row, the same target verbs rotated across
conditions, one speaker at a time, recording and transcribing, more fillers.]*
:::

## Your group's experiment

Groups of three, 10 minutes. Pick one:

1. **Which preposition:** *adhere to*, then *comply with*
2. **Elected or not:** *walked to the office*, then *replied to*
3. **Dative:** *gave Jordan* or *gave to Jordan*, then *explained ... to Chelsea*
4. **Pictures:** describe *watching birds*, then *listening to a singer*
5. **Case:** a language where the verb picks a case instead of a preposition

::: {.prompt}
Write down: what speakers say, what you count, what each account predicts.
:::

::: {.notes}
In groups of three, take ten minutes and design one experiment. Pick one of the
options on the slide. Write down what speakers will say, what you will count,
and what each account predicts.

*[Walk around. Leave five minutes for two groups to present.]*

Which preposition: *adhere* and *comply* both take a preposition, but different
ones. Speakers say *adhere to* on card 1 and *comply with* on card 2. The error
to count is *complied to*, the preposition from card 1 with the verb from card
2. This tests which preposition gets selected, in addition to whether one
appears at all.

Elected or not: *walked to the office* has a *to*, but *walk* does not require
it. If a card 1 with *walked to* helps speakers keep *replied to* as much as
*responded to* does, then what carries over does not depend on the verb
selecting *to*.

Dative: *Alex gave Jordan the explanation* and *Alex gave the explanation to
Jordan* are both fine, but *explain* only works with *to*. If someone says
*explained Chelsea* after *gave Jordan*, it could be the structure carrying over
or *to* being dropped. A simple sentence helps tell these apart: *explained the
problem Chelsea* keeps the original order, while *explained Chelsea the problem*
changes it. The extra slides have the cards for this one.

Pictures: instead of combining sentences, speakers describe a picture, for
example a woman listening to a singer. Before it, they describe a picture that
is easiest to describe with a verb that takes its object directly, like a man
watching birds. The advantage is that there is no sentence on the card to copy
*to* from, so any *to* comes from the speaker's own planning. The problem is
that speakers can pick other verbs, like *hearing* or *enjoying*. You need
pictures where *listen to* is the most likely description, and you have to count
other verbs separately.

Case: Turkish is one example. *Bak-* 'look at' takes the dative, and *gör-*
'see' takes the accusative. The case is pronounced on the noun, so if the case
from one verb carries over to the other, you can hear it. English relative
clauses like ours have no noun after *to*, so English gives us no case to hear.

A good version of any of these could become a final project.
:::

## Candidate verb pairs {.smaller}

| V + NP | V + PP | Sense to hold fixed |
|---|---|---|
| hear the singer | listen to the singer | perception vs. attention |
| answer the e-mail | reply / respond to the e-mail | responding to a message |
| watch the birds | look at the birds | visual attention |
| seek a solution | look for a solution | searching |
| request an extension | ask for an extension | requesting |
| obey the rules | abide by the rules | compliance |
| follow the protocol | adhere to the protocol | compliance |
| follow the regulations | comply with the regulations | compliance |
| obey Elizabeth | answer to Elizabeth | authority |
| trust Chelsea | confide in Chelsea | related acts |

Class materials; check each pair with the speakers you test

These are extra verb pairs for groups that want more items. Each row pairs a verb
that takes its object directly with a verb that takes a preposition, in a
similar sense. Some pairs are closer in meaning than others. Check each pair
with the speakers you test: *trust in Chelsea*, for example, is fine for many
people, so it should not automatically count as an error.
:::
